notes.meaning: King Jeroboam stood beside his new altar in Bethel to burn incense during a religious festival he had invented. Suddenly, an unnamed prophet arrived from Judah, driven by the direct power and command of the Lord. God sent this messenger at the exact moment the king was trying to act as his own priest.

Instead of addressing the king directly, the prophet spoke to the altar itself to show how stubborn the people had become. He announced that a future descendant of David named Josiah would tear down the altar and burn the bones of false priests upon it. This exact event took place more than three centuries later.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars view the phrase mentioning Josiah by name as a later editorial addition made after the prophecy was fulfilled.

notes.meaning: The prophet gave a miraculous sign that would happen right away to prove his long-term prophecy was true. He said the altar would break apart and its ashes would spill onto the ground. This demonstrated that God completely rejected Jeroboam's false system of worship.

Jeroboam was furious when he heard the judgment against his altar. He pointed toward the prophet and ordered his guards to seize him. At that very moment, the king's arm froze stiff and paralyzed, leaving him unable to pull it back.

Just as the prophet had said, the altar cracked apart and the ashes poured out onto the ground. This happened purely by God's power, without any human hand touching the stones. It proved beyond doubt that the man of God was speaking the truth.

The terrified king begged the prophet to pray for God to heal his paralyzed arm. The man of God showed great kindness by immediately praying for the man who had just tried to arrest him. God answered the prayer and restored the king's arm, offering Jeroboam another chance to repent.

Jeroboam invited the prophet to his house to eat a meal and receive a generous reward. In ancient times, eating together signaled friendship, fellowship, and mutual agreement. If the prophet accepted, it would look to the people as though he approved of the king's false religion.

The prophet firmly refused the king's offer. He stated that even if Jeroboam gave him half of all his royal possessions, he would not enter the king's house. He was determined not to eat bread or drink water in an idolatrous place.

The prophet explained that the Lord had given him very strict orders. He was commanded not to eat or drink anything in Bethel, and he had to return home by a different route. These rules showed God's complete rejection of the town's idolatry and kept the prophet from lingering.

The prophet obeyed the Lord's instructions and took another path home. By avoiding the road he had traveled before, he began his journey back to Judah without eating or drinking. At this point, he had faithfully resisted the king's pressure.

An older prophet was living in Bethel at that time. His sons had attended the king's ceremony and came home to report everything that had happened at the altar. They described the miracles and the bold message spoken against the king.
The old prophet asked his sons which way the visitor had gone. His sons had seen the path taken by the man of God and pointed it out. The father immediately decided to follow after him.

The old prophet told his sons to saddle his donkey without delay. Since the prophet from Judah was traveling on foot, riding a donkey would allow the older man to overtake him quickly. Once the animal was ready, he set out on the road.

The old prophet found the traveler resting under a well-known oak tree along the road. The man of God was likely weary, hungry, and thirsty from his journey under the heat. The older prophet asked if he was the man who had come from Judah, and the traveler confirmed he was.

The old prophet invited the traveler to come back home with him to eat a meal. He seemed eager to show hospitality and talk with a fellow prophet. However, accepting this invitation meant turning around and heading back into Bethel.

The man of God turned down the offer, just as he had done with the king earlier. Even though he was exhausted and hungry, he stood by what God had commanded. He repeated that he could not return or share food and water in that place.

The traveler repeated the exact message the Lord had given him. He was forbidden from eating bread, drinking water, or traveling back along the same path. He treated God's original instruction as absolute and binding.

The old prophet claimed that he also served the true God and that an angel had brought him a new command from the Lord. He insisted that the angel told him to bring the traveler home for a meal. The text plainly states that the old prophet was lying.

differ.view: God's clear revelation cannot be overturned by new private claims or supposed angelic messages, which points to the principle that scripture alone is the final authority for faith.

notes.meaning: The man of God believed the lie and went back to Bethel to eat and drink at the old prophet's house. He made a tragic mistake by trusting another person's claim instead of sticking to what God had told him directly. He allowed human persuasion to override God's clear word.

While both men were sitting at the table sharing their meal, the true word of the Lord came upon the old prophet. The very man who had spoken lies was now chosen by God to deliver an authentic message of judgment. This unexpected turn exposed the gravity of their disobedience.

The old prophet cried out to the traveler with a solemn declaration from the Lord. He announced that the man from Judah had defied God's direct command by returning. God held His own messenger strictly accountable for breaking his orders.

The sentence was announced: because he ate and drank in the forbidden place, his body would never be buried in his family tomb. In the ancient world, being denied burial with one's ancestors was viewed as a terrible tragedy and disgrace. This meant he would face an untimely death away from home.

After the meal ended, the old prophet saddled a donkey for his guest to ride. Even though a dreadful judgment had been spoken over him, the traveler set out on his journey home. The old prophet did not travel along with him.

As the man traveled along the road, a lion attacked and killed him. Instead of eating the corpse or attacking the donkey, the lion simply stood peacefully beside the body alongside the animal. This unusual behavior showed that the attack was a miraculous act of divine judgment rather than a random animal encounter.

Other travelers passed by on the highway and saw the lion and the donkey standing quietly beside the dead body. The lion did not threaten them as they walked past. When the travelers arrived in Bethel, they reported this astonishing sight to the people of the city.

When the old prophet heard the news, he immediately knew what had happened. He recognized that the deceased traveler was the prophet who had disobeyed God's command. He acknowledged that the Lord had sent the lion to fulfill the exact judgment spoken at the table.
The old prophet told his sons to saddle his donkey once again. His sons got the animal ready, and he set out to find the body. He went to recover the remains of the fallen prophet.

When he arrived, he found the body lying in the road, with the donkey and the lion still standing right beside it. The lion had not eaten the corpse or harmed the donkey. This remarkable scene confirmed to everyone present that God had directed the entire event.

The old prophet lifted the corpse, placed it on his donkey, and brought it back into his own city. He took responsibility for giving the man a proper burial and mourning over him. This action showed genuine sorrow and deep respect for the true prophet.

The old prophet buried the traveler in his own personal tomb. He and his household wept over him with the traditional funeral lament, "Oh, my brother!" In this way, the prophecy came true, because the man was buried far away from his ancestral home.

After the funeral, the old prophet instructed his sons that when he died, they must bury him in the very same tomb beside the man of God. He knew the prophet's words were completely reliable. He hoped that resting next to a true prophet would protect his own bones from future destruction.

The old prophet declared that every word spoken against the altar at Bethel and the high places would certainly come true. The swift punishment of the man of God had proved how seriously God takes His word. Centuries later, King Josiah carried out this exact judgment.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The phrase 'cities of Samaria' is widely seen as an editorial update by a later writer, since Samaria was not founded as the capital until the reign of King Omri decades later.

notes.meaning: Even after seeing the shattered altar, his withered hand, and the fate of the prophet, Jeroboam refused to turn from his wicked ways. He continued appointing ordinary men from any background to serve as priests at his shrines. Anyone who wanted the office was ordained, in complete disregard for God's law.

Jeroboam's stubborn disobedience became the defining sin of his royal house. This continual rebellion brought about the total destruction and extinction of his family line. His story stands as a lasting warning that resisting God's truth brings ruin.
